extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and educated readers/critics (Elizabethan/Renaissance literary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing and assessing poetry and drama: what makes heroic verse effective, the moral and mnemonic aims of poetry, technical requirements for verse and staging, and common faults to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroical poetry as the highest kind
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroical ... is the best and most accomplished kind, most capable and most fit to awake the thoughts from the sleep of idleness, to embrace honourable enterprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lofty images of worthies (e.g., Achilles, Æneas, Cyrus) to inflame the mind with desire to be worthy and to instruct how to be worthy; heroical poetry should set virtue and magnanimity before the reader in a way that makes virtue attractive and exemplary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must teach and move to truth/virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'doth not only teach and move to truth, but teacheth and moveth to the most high and excellent truth' and 'for instructing, is well nigh comparable to the philosopher; for moving, leaveth him behind him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good poem combines moral instruction with emotional persuasion: it should both inform (teach) and motivate (move) readers toward virtuous action. Evaluate poetry by its capacity to instruct and to move the affections toward the good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as maker: originality of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet only bringeth his own stuff, and doth not learn a conceit out of a matter, but maketh matter for a conceit; the poet maketh matter rather than borrowing wholly from subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value the poet's inventive power: poetry is creative making, not mere transcription. Assess the freshness of the poet's conceits and the extent to which the poem supplies its own matter rather than depending solely on external facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's moral harmlessness by description
rubrics_metrics.description: Since neither his description nor end containeth any evil, the thing described cannot be evil; the poet describeth for imaginative instruction, not to assert factual truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging alleged immorality in poetry, distinguish descriptive representation from endorsement; a poet's depiction of vice is not ipso facto a promotion of vice. Consider authorial intent and the poem's overall moral lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse is superior for memory and transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse far exceedeth prose in the knitting up of the memory ... words which are fittest for memory, are likewise most convenient for knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft lines with measured quantity, harmony, and internal ordering so that each word has a 'natural seat'—this aids memorability and the transmission of knowledge; use rhyme/measure as mnemonic aids, not mere ornament. Evidence: poets' verses serving as lifelong lessons; rules of arts compiled in verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versing/rhyming is not identical to true poesy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not rhyming and versing that maketh poesy; one may be a poet without versing, and a versifier without poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate technical versification with poetic quality. Evaluate by imaginative power, moral and emotional effect, and craft, not by mere presence of rhyme or regular meter. Avoid thinking versifying alone is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry (fiction) does not constitute lying
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet never affirmeth; to lie is to affirm that to be true which is false: the poet telleth not for true but for what should or should not be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fictional elements as imaginative examples, not false claims. Poets call the Muses and present inventions; therefore, fictional narration should not be judged on the same standard as historians or scientists who assert factual truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse of poetry is a misuse by readers, not necessarily a fault of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Though poesy may be abused ... the abuse shall not give reproach to the abused; contrariwise, whatsoever being abused, doth most harm, being rightly used doth most good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a poem accused of corrupting readers, weigh the poem's intended (right) use and its capacity for good; do not condemn the art because of potential misuse. Compare to other arts that can be abused (medicine, law, scripture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's necessary capacities: art, imitation, and exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: That Dædalus ... hath three wings to bear itself up into the air of due commendation; that is art, imitation, and exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good poet needs (1) art—technical knowledge of craft; (2) imitation—study of models; and (3) exercise—practice. Evaluate poets on whether they cultivate all three and avoid sloppy habits (e.g., writing as if already knowing everything).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order matter and words: avoid 'quodlibet' composition
rubrics_metrics.description: There being two principal parts, matter to be expressed by words, and words to express the matter, in neither we use art or imitation rightly. Our matter is 'quodlibet' ... never marshalling it into any assured rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with disciplined selection and arrangement of matter; do not assemble miscellaneous lines that simply beget each other. Assess structure: is there an assured rank and coherence of matter, or a confused mass of words driven only by rhyme?

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy: unity of place and time (stage constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage should always represent but one place; and the uttermost time presupposed in it ... should be ... but one day; many days and many places are inartificially imagined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For dramatic representation, keep to a single place and a limited time-frame (per Aristotle) unless a deliberate artistic reason justifies deviation. Judge plays that shift place/time as violating theatrical art if they force constant scene-setting by players.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should begin at the principal point (not 'ab ovo')
rubrics_metrics.description: They must not, as Horace saith, begin 'ab ovo,' but they must come to the principal point of that one action which they will represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic narratives should start close to the crucial action rather than narrating long backstory onstage. Use offstage report (messengers/nuntius) to relate distant or prior events so the play focuses on the essential tragic moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy adheres to laws of poesy, not slavish history
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is tied to the laws of poesy, and not of history; not bound to follow the story, but having liberty either to feign a quite new matter, or to frame the history to the most tragical convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt historical material for poetic ends; prioritize tragic unity, moral and emotional effects, and dramatic necessities over literal chronological accuracy. Judge historical fidelity less strictly than dramatic efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish representing from reporting (use of messenger)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many things may be told, which cannot be showed ... the ancients took by some 'Nuntius' to recount things done in former time, or other place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative devices (messengers, reports) to convey events not suitable for onstage representation. Evaluate dramaturgy by appropriate choices between showing and telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate mingling of comedy and tragedy (decorum)
rubrics_metrics.description: All their plays be neither right tragedies nor right comedies, mingling kings and clowns ... thrust in the clown by head and shoulders to play a part in majestical matters, with neither decency nor discretion; so as neither the admiration and commiseration, nor the right sportfulness, is by their mongrel tragi-comedy obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain genre decorum: do not insert buffoonery into high tragic scenes unless done with delicate art; comedy should produce refined delight, not mere scurrility or gross laughter. Judge mixtures of tones by whether they undermine the intended emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's aim: delight (not merely laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our comedians think there is no delight without laughter, which is very wrong; for though laughter may come with delight, yet cometh it not of delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess comedies by their capacity to produce pleasure and moral or social insight, not by the raw quantity of laughter. Prefer wit and sustained delight over coarse mirth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical faults in stagecraft to avoid (places, times, monsters, armies)
rubrics_metrics.description: You shall have Asia of the one side, and Afric of the other ... three ladies walk to gather flowers, and then ... news of shipwreck in the same place ... a hideous monster with fire and smoke ... two armies fly in, represented with four swords and bucklers ... two hours' space [covering many years].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contrived stage devices that force spectators to accept impossible simultaneous locales or compressed chronologies; do not rely on cheap spectacle (monsters, token armies) that break plausibility. Judge plays harshly when such devices cause confusion or strain credibility.
